{{short description|Tetrahedron whose edge lengths, face areas and volume are all integers}}
A '''Heronian tetrahedron'''{{r|mp13}} (also called a '''Heron tetrahedron'''{{r|cm06}} or '''perfect pyramid'''{{r|b92}}) is a [[tetrahedron]] whose edge lengths, face areas and volume are all [[integer]]s. The faces must therefore all be [[Heronian triangle]]s (named for [[Hero of Alexandria]]).
Every Heronian tetrahedron can be arranged in [[Euclidean space]] so that its vertex coordinates are also integers.{{r|mp13}}

==Examples==
[[File:Heronian_birectangular_tetrahedron.svg|thumb|250px|[[Isometric projection]] of Euler's Heronian birectangular tetrahedron in its [[minimum bounding box]] ]]
An example known to [[Leonhard Euler]] is a Heronian [[Schläfli orthoscheme|birectangular tetrahedron]], a tetrahedron with a path of three edges parallel to the three coordinate axes and with all faces being [[right triangle]]s. The lengths of the edges on the path of axis-parallel edges are 153, 104, and 672, and the other three edge lengths are 185, 680, and 697, forming four right triangle faces described by the [[Pythagorean triple]]s (153,104,185), (104,672,680), (153,680,697), and (185,672,697).{{r|gardner}}

Eight examples of Heronian tetrahedra were discovered in 1877 by [[Reinhold Hoppe]].{{r|h77}}

[[117 (number)|117]] is the smallest possible length of the longest edge of a perfect tetrahedron with integral edge lengths. Its other edge lengths are 51, 52, 53, 80 and 84.{{r|b92}} 8064 is the smallest possible volume (and 6384 is the smallest possible surface area) of a perfect tetrahedron. The integral edge lengths of a Heronian tetrahedron with this volume and surface area are 25, 39, 56, 120, 153 and 160.{{r|p03}}

In 1943, E. P. Starke published another example, in which two faces are [[isosceles triangle]]s with base 896 and sides 1073, and the other two faces are also isosceles with base 990 and the same sides.{{r|s43}} However, Starke made an error in reporting its volume which has become widely copied.{{r|cm06}} The correct volume is {{val|124185600}}, twice the number reported by Starke.{{r|crux}}

Sascha Kurz has used computer search algorithms to find all Heronian tetrahedra with longest edge length at most {{val|600000}}.{{r|k08}}

==Classification, infinite families, and special types of tetrahedron==
A [[regular tetrahedron]] (one with all faces being equilateral) cannot be a Heronian tetrahedron because, for regular tetrahedra whose edge lengths are integers, the face areas and volume are [[irrational number]]s.{{r|c73}} For the same reason no Heronian tetrahedron can have an [[equilateral triangle]] as one of its faces.{{r|b92}}

There are infinitely many Heronian tetrahedra, and more strongly infinitely many Heronian [[disphenoid]]s, tetrahedra in which all faces are congruent and each pair of opposite sides has equal lengths. In this case, there are only three edge lengths needed to describe the tetrahedron, rather than six, and the triples of lengths that define Heronian tetrahedra can be characterized using an [[elliptic curve]].{{r|b92|g07}} There are also infinitely many Heronian tetrahedra with a cycle of four equal edge lengths, in which all faces are [[isosceles triangle]]s.{{r|cm06}}

There are also infinitely many Heronian birectangular tetrahedra. One method for generating tetrahedra of this type derives the axis-parallel edge lengths <math>a</math>, <math>b</math>, and <math>c</math> from two equal [[Sums of powers|sums of fourth powers]]
:<math>p^4+s^4=q^4+r^4</math>
using the formulas
:<math>a=\bigl|(pq)^2-(rs)^2\bigr|,</math>
:<math>b=\bigl|2pqrs\bigr|,</math>
:<math>c=\bigl|(pr)^2-(qs)^2\bigr|.</math>
For instance, the tetrahedron derived in this way from an identity of [[Leonhard Euler]], <math>59^4+158^4=133^4+134^4</math>, has <math>a</math>, <math>b</math>, and <math>c</math> equal to {{val|386678175}}, {{val|332273368}}, and {{val|379083360}}, with the [[hypotenuse]] of right triangle <math>ab</math> equal to {{val|509828993}}, the hypotenuse of right triangle <math>bc</math> equal to {{val|504093032}}, and the hypotenuse of the remaining two sides equal to {{val|635318657}}.{{r|crux}} For these tetrahedra, <math>a</math>, <math>b</math>, and <math>c</math> form the edge lengths of an [[Euler brick#Almost-perfect cuboids|almost-perfect cuboid]], a rectangular cuboid in which the sides, two of the three face diagonals, and the body diagonal are all integers.{{r|gardner}}

A complete classification of all Heronian tetrahedra remains unknown.{{r|mp13|cm06}}

==Heronian trirectangular tetrahedron==
No example of a Heronian [[trirectangular tetrahedron]] had been found and no one has proven that none exist.

The existence of a solution to the Heronian trirectangular tetrahedron problem is equivalent to the existence of a solution to the [[Perfect cuboid]] problem, and conversely, the existence of a Perfect cuboid implies the existence of a Heronian trirectangular tetrahedron.<ref name=Belogourov>Alexander Belogourov, On the Equivalence of the Perfect Cuboid and Heronian Trirectangular Tetrahedron Problems, https://www.academia.edu/83027639/On_the_Equivalence_of_the_Perfect_Cuboid_and_Heronian_Trirectangular_Tetrahedron_Problems</ref> If there exists a Heronian trirectangular tetrahedron with three orthogonal edges <math>a, b, c</math>, then the cuboid with edges <math>(ab, ac, bc)</math> has integer face diagonals and an integer space diagonal, making it a Perfect cuboid. And vice versa, if there exists a Perfect сuboid with edges <math>a, b, c</math>, then the tetrahedron with orthogonal integer edges <math>(ab, ac, bc)</math> at a common vertex is Heronian.

==Related shapes==
An alternative definition of Heronian triangles is that they can be formed by gluing together two [[Pythagorean triple|integer right triangle]]s along a common side.
This definition has also been generalized to three dimensions, leading to a different class of tetrahedra that have also been called Heron tetrahedra.{{r|lin11}}
